title: Is the craft following the command well?
summary: Use Graph and ordinary-flight Step Response to separate tracking, damping, sustained-error, Feedforward, saturation, and evidence quality—without turning one symptom into one gain change.
questions: Does gyro response lag, lead, overshoot, or rise slowly relative to setpoint?
What do P, I, D, and Feedforward contribute to the recorded response?
Are filtering, motor headroom, excitation, and comparison quality good enough to support a PID hypothesis?

blocks.text: Good control response is not merely fast, and definitely not 'largest number wins'. Read the recorded signal order in Graph, use ordinary-flight Step Response for repeated behaviour, and keep every PID-F interpretation conditional on filter evidence, actuator headroom, and the quality of the flight input.

blocks.title: Establish filter evidence first
blocks.text: Residual D-term noise and filter delay constrain meaningful PID interpretation. Confirm what remains after filtering and whether motor commands retain headroom before treating an overshoot, lag, or oscillation as a controller-balance problem.

blocks.caption: Controller roles in the recorded response
rows: P
Responds to current processed rate error and contributes tracking authority.
Its effect cannot be separated from D balance, common gain, saturation, and plant dynamics by one peak.
I
Accumulates processed error to correct sustained mismatch.
Relax, anti-windup, leak, saturation, and firmware behaviour make slow correction a hypothesis, not an I-only diagnosis.
D
Responds to gyro change to add damping.
It is high-frequency-sensitive; recorded output reflects both configured gain and noise passing through the filter path.
Feedforward
Responds to setpoint change before feedback error has to build.
It is command-derived, not another feedback-error gain, and can interact with damping and saturation.

steps: Choose System Response and select Step Response.
Use a flight range with sufficient setpoint and filtered-gyro excitation.
Compare axes, accepted and candidate window counts, normalized peak, half-response latency, and 10–90% rise time.
Split low- and high-rate windows when the recording supports both rather than averaging unlike moves together.
Add reference logs only when manoeuvres, rates, hardware, filters, battery state, and evidence quality are reasonably comparable.

blocks.title: Balance is not the same as gain

blocks.text: P:D balance primarily changes damping behaviour, while common P/D scaling changes controller authority without intentionally changing that balance. P:I balance concerns sustained-error correction, and Feedforward concerns anticipatory tracking. Modern nonlinear features, filters, saturation, and mechanics mean none of these relationships is a complete plant model.

blocks.title: Keep yaw separate
blocks.text: Yaw has different authority and plant dynamics from roll and pitch, and it commonly uses a different D-term strategy. Do not copy roll/pitch damping expectations or gain relationships onto yaw without axis-specific evidence.

blocks.title: Comparison needs comparable excitation
blocks.text: Different manoeuvres, rates, battery state, props, payload, wind, filters, and accepted-window counts can change the estimate. Reference overlays reveal differences; they do not create a controlled experiment after the fact.
